topic: The Curious Link: Block Collisions and the Digits of Pi

sections.title: The Hook: The Bouncing Block Paradox
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: two blocks of different masses on a frictionless surface, with a wall on the left. Block A (mass m) sits between the wall and Block B (mass M). We count the number of collisions.
sections.example: A small ant (Block A) and a large elephant (Block B) sliding on ice towards a solid stone wall.

sections.title: Prerequisites: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly explain that in elastic collisions, both Kinetic Energy and Momentum are conserved. Use a vector diagram to show how velocity vectors change after impact, emphasizing the velocity reflection rule.
sections.example: Visualizing the velocity vectors of the ant and elephant as arrows changing direction upon collision, represented by a reflection across an energy-conserving boundary.

sections.title: The Scaling Connection: Phase Space
sections.content: Explain that the collision system can be mapped to a billiard ball bouncing inside a circular boundary. The 'angle' of the collision represents the digits of Pi. As mass M increases by powers of 100, the collision count increases by digits of Pi.
sections.example: An animation showing a light ray bouncing inside a circle; as the mass ratio M/m grows, the 'path' of the collision count converges to 3.1415...

sections.title: Deep Dive: The 1:100 Ratio
sections.content: Demonstrate that if Block B is 100^n times heavier than Block A, the total number of collisions is exactly the first n+1 digits of Pi.
sections.example: Table graphic: 1:1 ratio = 3 collisions; 1:100 ratio = 31 collisions; 1:10,000 ratio = 314 collisions.

sections.title: Synthesis & Summary
sections.content: Summarize how a mechanical, discrete system (blocks hitting) generates a transcendental, continuous constant (Pi). Reiterate that the physics of conservation laws creates a geometric shadow of Pi.
sections.example: Final visual: A computer simulation of blocks colliding, where the collision counter progressively spells out 3.14159...
